Furthermore, ReRAMLE is shown to be a generalizable solution that can handle various reward function types, including linear and nonlinear functions. The proposed method has also been applied to more complex problems, such as contextual multi-armed bandits and contextual linear bandits, with promising results. Overall, ReRAMLE offers a simple yet effective solution for neural contextual bandits that outperforms existing methods while providing improved interpretability and sample complexity. By recalibrating jet energy corrections to account for flavor-dependent effects, the D{\O} collaboration found that their initial top mass measurement would need to be revised by 0.7-1.4 GeV if these corrections were properly applied. This recalibration was found to significantly impact jet energy corrections with high $b$-jet energy, leading to a substantial effect on the top mass measurement. This discrepancy arises from the initial calibration's reliance on $b$-jet energy, which can be mitigated by using alternative jet energy corrections. Furthermore, the initial calibration's impact on the $b$-jet energy scale uncertainty is noteworthy, as it can cause a 50% increase in the uncertainty of the top mass measurement. This recalibration's effects on the D{\O} lepton+jets top mass measurement are comparable to the statistical uncertainty, suggesting a potential need to reevaluate the current top mass measurement. This recalibration's effects on the D{\O} dilepton and semi-leptonic top mass measurements are significantly smaller. Recent advancements in child activity recognition have been driven by the growing need for precise monitoring of child motion patterns. The task of matching image pairs that are visually similar can be a difficult challenge, particularly when the images are of scenes that are poorly lit.  This is because the standard methods used for this purpose are typically based on features that are derived from high-quality images, but are then applied to lower quality images.  This can lead to issues with consistency in performance, as the features may not accurately capture the true relationships between the images.  To address this problem, we have compiled a dataset of pairs of images taken under different exposure settings from the same scene, which we call the Dark Pair Dataset.  This dataset was created by intentionally over- and under-exposing the images, while keeping everything else the same.  We then tested our dataset with a variety of state-of-the-art image matching methods and found that they performed significantly worse on the under-exposed images compared to the standard images.  To address this, we have developed a new method that can match images even when the standard features are not reliable.  This method, which we call Darknet, uses a neural network to learn the features from the standard images and then applies this to the under-exposed images.  We show that this method can match the performance of the standard image matching methods even when the images are severely under-exposed.  The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/berndpfromm/dark-pair-dataset.  This work was presented at the 2020 International Conference on Computer Vision. In recent years, graph embedding algorithms have been widely used to learn representations of graphs, particularly useful for tasks such as link prediction. However, these algorithms have limitations when applied to multiplex graphs, which consist of multiple interconnected layers. Currently, there is a lack of efficient methods for link prediction on multiplex graphs, which hinders their practical application. To address this issue, we introduce MultiSAGE, a novel algorithm that learns a shared space representation of multiplex graphs, taking into account the characteristics of each individual layer. By doing so, MultiSAGE enables the prediction of links across all layers of the graph, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between nodes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MultiSAGE in extracting complex relationships between nodes, even in cases where the underlying patterns are difficult to discern. Our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods for link prediction on both synthetic and real-world multiplex graphs, with the source code available on GitHub at https://github.com/UMBCVision/MultiSAGE. Cubic spline interpolation is a widely used technique in computer-aided design and data processing, but its application can be compromised when the underlying data exhibits sharp changes in values. In such cases, the method may not accurately capture the essential characteristics of the data, particularly when the values are not arranged in order. To address this limitation, we introduce a new monotone cubic spline interpolation method that preserves data values' ordering, thus providing a more reliable estimate of function derivatives. The proposed approach avoids the L2 norm-based smoothing that can alter the original data's ordered sequence, instead relying on a different smoothing technique that maintains the data's monotonicity. Additionally, we establish the theoretical foundation for the method, including error bounds for interpolation and approximation, as well as convergence rates for various types of data. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in preserving complex details in images and functional relationships in function approximation, thus offering a valuable tool for data processing and computational applications. Recent studies have highlighted the susceptibility of deep learning models to adversarial attacks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method for generating adversarial samples that exploits non-semantic features in high-dimensional image data. Our approach involves replacing specific feature clusters with alternative ones during the forward pass, thus inducing adversarial behavior without altering the model's input class labels. By employing this technique, we can create adversarial samples that appear nearly indistinguishable from their original counterparts. Furthermore, we can also leverage this method to conceal images by substituting meaningful features with deceptive ones during the forward pass, thus thwarting model predictions. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method on both white-box and black-box models. For instance, we were able to decrease the accuracy of a pre-trained Inception-BN model on the CIFAR10 dataset by a significant margin, while maintaining a high level of visual fidelity. Additionally, we were able to mislead a black-box model to produce incorrect predictions, effectively concealing a substantial portion of the original image. Our approach offers a promising solution to mitigate the vulnerability of deep learning models to adversarial attacks. However, we also identify potential risks associated with this technique, such as its misuse for malicious purposes. To mitigate these risks, we recommend that future work focus on developing detection mechanisms for this type of attack. Our code and experimental results are publicly available for further study. Our results show that models can still maintain high accuracy on unseen data despite being equipped with Learnability Lock. Moreover, our approach can effectively limit overfitting, even when the model is fully utilized. Notably, our approach outperforms existing data obfuscation techniques that compromise model performance. Finally, we have successfully applied Learnability Lock to a large pre-trained GAN model, allowing for the selective control of learnable parameters. Deep learning models have been found to be susceptible to manipulative tactics that compromise their reliability in real-world applications. In this study, novel methods are developed to deceive machine learning models used for detecting fraud in e-commerce transactions and identifying imbalanced classes within datasets. These tactics leverage the underlying structure of tabular data, specifically linear relationships, to increase their effectiveness. Additionally, the proposed methods demonstrate their robustness in various deep learning frameworks and models, including simple and complex configurations. Experimental results indicate that these tactics can effectively mislead even the best-performing models, suggesting the need for enhanced security measures in real-world applications. Furthermore, the proposed methods can be adapted for both defensive and adversarial purposes, such as training a model to resist such attacks or testing the resilience of existing models against malicious inputs. The developed adversarial attacks are implemented in a Python library called AdvTab, which is accessible through GitHub. The accompanying code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/ParitoshParmar/AdvTab. The findings of this study are presented in a self-contained and accessible manner, making it suitable for researchers and practitioners with varying levels of expertise in the field. The primary contribution of this study is the development of a novel, universal framework for crafting adversarial attacks that can be applied to other tabular datasets. The proposed methods are expected to facilitate the development of more robust and reliable machine learning models, especially in applications involving imbalanced classes and real-world data. The authors also provide recommendations for future work, such as exploring the connection between adversarial and robust training, and developing more effective and efficient attacks. The proposed methods are not limited to fraud detection and can be adapted for other applications, such as predicting income levels or housing prices. The developed library, AdvTab, is designed to be versatile and can be easily adapted for other applications, such as image or text-based attacks. This research introduces a novel method for approximating statistical models in a way that protects individual data points. The proposed approach optimizes an objective function that represents the model's likelihood, modified to incorporate differential privacy. However, due to the added perturbation, the likelihood function becomes less reliable. To address this issue, we developed a two-step method that uses an MCMC algorithm to generate candidate model parameters. The candidates are then evaluated against a rough estimate of the model's accuracy, and the best fit is selected. The proposed approach is demonstrated to work effectively on various models, including generalized linear and logistic, and shown to produce accurate results for both location and systematic models. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for constructing confidence intervals that provides accurate coverage even in cases with limited data points. The creation of photorealistic 3D faces is a complex task that involves generating multiple modalities such as meshes and images, each having distinct structures and textures. Current methods either generate individual modalities in isolation or using a common latent code, but this leads to issues like the mesh not matching an existing image or vice versa, or the image not matching a corresponding mesh. To address these problems, we introduce a new framework called trunk-branch generative adversarial networks, consisting of a common latent code for both modalities and individual paths for each. The common path generates shared features shared between modalities, while individual paths refine and match specific features unique to each modality. The proposed approach is validated through experiments and demonstrates its effectiveness in generating consistent 3D faces with detailed textures. The accompanying code is available on GitHub. \\

Timed automata are a fundamental model for analyzing real-time systems. The reachability problem, which involves determining all states within a system, has been extensively studied. Notably, it was shown to be PSPACE-complete. To address this issue, researchers introduced a variant called pushdown timed automata, defined by a context-free host language and timed automata constraints. The reachability problem for this model is undecidable, prompting the exploration of its parameterized complexity. This study investigates the complexity of reachability in a specific context: given a pushdown timed automaton, its host language, and a constraint automaton, identify all states from which the constraint automaton's language is reachable. The proposed algorithms demonstrate the decidability of this problem within single-exponential time under certain conditions, such as a bounded number of control states or a bounded number of states within a given reachability class. The algorithms' complexity is further analyzed under different conditions, such as a bounded number of edges or vertices. Additionally, a tool called TimedPDPA has been developed to verify parametric timed properties in pushdown process algebras. The tool's implementation has achieved single-exponential time performance. The study also presents a reduction from a more general problem to the reachability problem, establishing a connection to the single-exponential time complexity. The proposed algorithms have been implemented and evaluated on a large dataset of instances. The results demonstrate the efficiency of the algorithms on a subset of instances, but their performance degrades as the number of states within the reachability class increases. To mitigate this, a heuristic approach has been introduced to reduce the search space, leading to improved performance on a larger dataset. The proposed algorithms have been compared to a state-of-the-art tool called TAPAJO. While TAPAJO is more efficient on a smaller dataset, the new heuristic results in comparable performance on a larger dataset. Overall, the study presents a significant improvement in the single-exponential time complexity of reachability in pushdown timed automata. This new scaling theory provides a quantitative connection between the rate of energy release and the statistical properties of slip at frictional interfaces, offering a framework to explain the observed variability in earthquake statistics. However, these networks of interconnected wires can be susceptible to attacks, specifically coherence violations, which can be exploited to gain unauthorized access.  This paper examines the risks and consequences of such attacks, including data corruption and the potential for a backdoor, and proposes methods to prevent them.  Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of implementing a low-cost, hardware-based solution to mitigate the effects of these attacks.  This study provides the first analysis of the vulnerability of interposers to coherence violations and the need for protection mechanisms.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that a hardware-based approach is effective in preventing data corruption caused by these attacks, although it may be impractical for widespread use due to the need for specialized hardware.  On the other hand, a software-based approach is also possible, but its effectiveness is limited to preventing data corruption caused by certain types of attacks, not all types.  This paper highlights the need for further research into the protection of 3D systems-on-chip, including the development of low-cost, effective solutions to prevent data corruption and facilitate secure operations. The adoption of feature toggles is a software engineering technique that allows developers to work on incompatible features simultaneously by enabling and disabling them easily. Feature toggles usage has been on the rise, but their effectiveness in preventing conflicts and testing new features remains to be seen. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between feature toggles usage and various software metrics, including the frequency of conflicts, tests, and bug reports, across 1,200 open-source Java repositories. The findings revealed that feature toggles usage is associated with reduced instances of conflicts, tests, and bug reports. Specifically, when a feature toggle is used, the frequency of conflicts decreases by 1.4 times, tests increase by 4.5 times, and bug reports decrease by 0.9 times. The results also showed that feature toggles usage is more prevalent in larger repositories, contributing to fewer conflicts and bug reports. However, the study found that feature toggles usage is not significantly correlated with the number of tests performed. The results provide insights for researchers and practitioners to improve feature toggles usage and reduce conflicts in software development. Based on the study, a set of guidelines for feature toggles implementation and potential areas for future research have been established. Pandemics pose a significant threat to public health and economies worldwide.
Effective pandemic response requires timely and accurate modeling, which can be achieved through mathematical models that integrate real-world data. This approach enables researchers to simulate various scenarios, including anticipated and unforeseen developments, to inform data-informed decision-making. This article showcases several data-driven models for pandemic response across three distinct phases: initial mitigation efforts, ongoing prevention measures, and post-pandemic recovery. These models utilize real-world data and statistical techniques to provide valuable insights for policymakers and the public. By leveraging data-driven insights, data science can play a pivotal role in shaping the global response to and recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of data-driven approaches in addressing the complex challenges posed by pandemics. Further advancements in data science and mathematics are necessary to optimize pandemic response, and ongoing efforts to develop robust and adaptable models will facilitate a swift global recovery. been developed for efficient skin lesion detection. Our proposed distributed
learning approach leverages data from wearable health devices, such as smartwatches
and mobile cameras, to automatically classify skin lesions and alert users to
potentially life-threatening cancers. By utilizing advanced techniques like
transfer learning and deep learning, our system can effectively identify cancer
lesions and notify users of potential health risks. Our research has demonstrated
that our model can achieve high accuracy in cancer detection, with an impressive
AUC-ROC of 0.942. This innovative personal health assistant has the potential to
serve as an effective early warning system for skin cancer, empowering users to
take prompt action and seek medical attention when necessary. Our approach also
enables efficient model training and deployment on edge devices, facilitating fast
processing of skin images and immediate alerts. By integrating health and

We introduce choice trees, a simple and expressive framework that allows the representation of various types of recursive and non-deterministic programs. The definition of choice trees mirrors the design of recursive programs, making their formalization in Coq straightforward. We demonstrate that choice trees effectively represent non-deterministic programs with a partial function semantics, leading to a complete characterization of the partial functions they define. Furthermore, we show that choice trees can model impure, stateful programs, and their semantics, leveraging the connection between stateful choice trees and a specific kind of automaton. The definition of choice trees is also amenable to a concise proof that any recursive data type with a non-deterministic semantics can be represented as a choice tree. We present a novel self-supervised image denoising approach called Decay2Distill, which enhances the performance of supervised methods by incorporating self-supervision. This method works by adding a noise decay schedule during training, which forces the denoising model to prioritize clean image features over noisy ones. As a result, the model can be distilled into a noise-free version that can be used for supervised denoising without decay. Our approach outperforms existing methods in PSNR and SSIM metrics, achieving state-of-the-art results in some cases, without relying on additional supervision or hyperparameters. Moreover, our method offers improved robustness against adversarial attacks and better performance on low-light images. Notably, our method is the first fully self-supervised denoising technique capable of matching the performance of supervised methods. The mass function of galaxy clusters is a key factor in determining cosmological models. 
This paper examines the influence of theoretical and observational uncertainties on the mass function of the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich desienable (SZ) sample. 
We find that the mass function uncertainty primarily stems from the uncertainty in the scaling relation between the SZ and stellar mass, and to a lesser extent from the mass-temperature relation. 
We also investigate the impact of other uncertainties such as those in the cosmological model, and the mass function of the sample. 
Our results indicate that the uncertainty in the scaling relation primarily affects the slope of the SZ mass function, and has a lesser effect on its normalization.

Cancer progression is significantly influenced by spatial factors, which are often studied using individual-based models that capture the complex interactions between cells and their environment. However, simulating these interactions over large spaces or long periods can be computationally expensive due to the high number of cells involved. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a new approach called OG-SPACE, a stochastic simulation tool designed to enhance the efficiency of spatial modeling in cancer evolution. OG-SPACE optimizes computational performance by reducing the number of cells simulated and leveraging approximation techniques to maintain accuracy. Through rigorous testing, the tool demonstrated a significant reduction in computational time, achieving speedups of up to 100 times without compromising results. OG-SPACE is now available as an open-source package, further enhancing its accessibility to the scientific community. With its ease of use and robust performance, the tool is poised to facilitate the rapid exploration of complex spatial models in cancer progression and other biological processes. OG-SPACE can be accessed at github.com/IMMB-BR/OG-SPACE. Further information can be found at the associated website, https://imm-benin.org/og-space. A new, uncomplicated pruning approach is proposed that focuses on re-allocating computational resources from less critical network paths to more essential ones. This straightforward method requires no prior knowledge of the target environment and can be applied to various architectures without modification. It achieves state-of-the-art results, matching or exceeding the performance of more complex pruning methods across a range of image classification tasks. Notably, the proposed approach retains more of the original network's weights during the pruning process, which makes them more useful for fine-tuning. This characteristic allows it to perform better when applied to other domains, a common scenario in which models are initially pre-trained and then adapted to specific tasks. Our findings suggest that pruning should not necessarily result in significant weight pruning, but rather in a strategic reallocation of resources to the most critical paths. This reallocation can be achieved through a simple thresholding technique that identifies and prioritizes the most important network paths. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach not only outperforms other straightforward pruning methods but also rivals the performance of more sophisticated pruning algorithms. Our implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/locuslab/ResourceReallocation. We also provide a video overview at https://youtu.be/8QsQ7QsQ7QsQ. A significant challenge in 3D semantic segmentation is efficiently processing large point clouds. To address this, we propose ParaNet, a novel, parallel network architecture designed to process point clouds in parallel. By representing point clouds as regular grids, rather than sparse, noisy points, ParaNet leverages the power of 2D image segmentation networks. Our approach enables the application of point cloud registration techniques to align the point cloud with its regular representation, which is then used to train ParaNet. Experimental results demonstrate that ParaNet outperforms state-of-the-art 3D point cloud segmentation networks and achieves a 6.4 times speed increase over PointNet++. Additionally, a software framework called GridNet democratizes the use of 2D segmentation networks for 3D point cloud segmentation, offering a more accessible solution. Our results show that ParaNet achieves comparable performance to PointNet++ on various datasets, often with better results. Furthermore, experiments with limited data highlight the framework's ability to produce robust point cloud segmenters with minimal training data. We introduce ASR2K, a pioneering system that provides speech recognition capabilities 
for approximately 2000 under-resourced languages. The system combines a unique 
approach to text generation through a sequence-to-sequence framework with a novel 
integration of cross-lingual phonetic transfer. Leveraging vast multilingual 
text data, ASR2K is capable of generating spoken content for numerous languages 
without relying on available labeled audio data. The system's performance is 
evaluated on 20 languages using the Wikitext dataset, and the results indicate that 
ASR2K can accurately transcribe spoken content with an average accuracy of 51.7 
WER. Furthermore, ASR2K's adaptability is demonstrated by its ability to improve 
transcription accuracy for languages with limited training data, achieving a WER of 
30.3. The open-source code for ASR2K is now publicly available for further 
research and development. The accompanying website provides additional 
demonstrations and information. The authors are eager to collaborate with the 
research community to continue advancing ASR2K's capabilities and expanding its 
applicability to even more languages. The system's potential to democratize speech 
recognition capabilities for historically under-resourced languages is also discussed.

Pretrained multilingual language models, such as Multilingual BERT (mBERT), exhibit
the ability to process multiple languages without requiring explicit training.
However, the mechanisms behind this ability are still poorly understood.
This study delves into mBERT's internal representation by analyzing its ability
to predict fine-grained linguistic features across languages.
We demonstrate that mBERT's performance in a specific task, masked word language
modelling, is heavily reliant on initial agreement in word representations,
resulting in improved accuracy for non-identical labels.
Notably, the model's ability to predict fine-grained labels is surprisingly
similar to its performance in predicting less granular labels.
This finding suggests that mBERT's cross-lingual representation learning is
driven by a two-stage process, where initial word representations are used to
generalize across languages and subsequent predictions build on these learned
representations.
The implications of these findings are further explored in the context of
downstream tasks. Overall, this study sheds light on the cross-lingual
representation learning capabilities of pre-trained multilingual language models. Cover

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have led to the widespread adoption of contrastive methods in various domains, particularly in collaborative filtering. However, prior research has largely overlooked the impact of user and item biases, which are crucial factors influencing recommendation outcomes. To bridge this gap, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the effect of bias in contrastive methods and develop a novel, bias-aware approach that integrates margins into the contrastive loss. By leveraging this method, we can dynamically adjust the similarity between positive and negative pairs, thereby optimizing the performance of contrastive-based recommender systems. Our proposed framework, BiCon, is evaluated on multiple real-world datasets and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the effect of bias in contrastive methods through the lens of margin theory. This study delves into permutations that steer clear of specific patterns defined by undirected bipartite graphs. To illustrate this concept further, we examine a particular case involving the pattern 231 without the aid of its characteristic matrix. Additionally, we present recurrence relations or explicit formulas for the counts of permutations evading these unique patterns when they can be defined using a straightforward approach. Moreover, we also investigate the total sum of the permutation counts that avoid these specific patterns and establish a connection between this total sum and particular cases involving the association schemes found in the bipartite graphs. To facilitate this exploration, we leverage the concept of group actions and use explicit examples to demonstrate the application of this approach to several undirected bipartite graphs. In this research, we develop an innovative policy optimization approach for constrained Markov decision processes that achieves guaranteed and rapid convergence under specific conditions. Traditional policy gradient methods often struggle to balance reward and constraint satisfaction. To address this, we utilize a logarithmic barrier function, which modifies the objective to emphasize constraint compliance. However, directly optimizing this modified objective can be challenging due to slow convergence. To overcome this issue, we introduce a new policy optimization algorithm that achieves fast convergence under mild assumptions. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we optimize without constraints using a policy gradient method; then, we adjust the objective by introducing a penalty term derived from the natural policy gradient method, which ensures a guaranteed lower bound on constraint violation. Notably, our algorithm does not require full access to the Hessian of the objective, and its convergence speed depends only on the growth rate of the reward, not its magnitude. Furthermore, our approach is scalable and efficient, and theoretical and empirical results confirm its global convergence under certain conditions. Our findings also demonstrate the benefits of our approach in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality. Our research provides a significant step towards developing policy optimization techniques with guaranteed fast convergence. A method to calculate the physical quantities of gas in the interstellar medium is called the hydrodynamics method. This approach typically requires knowledge of the properties of gas in the medium, such as heating and cooling rates. These rates are often determined using radiation fields from stars, which can be complex due to their varying properties. We investigated how different types of radiation fields impact heating and cooling rates by comparing observations with various radiation field models, including ones based on starlight, dust grain glow, and both combined. We found that heating and cooling rates are significantly affected by the type of radiation field used. For example, heating rates varied by up to 50% and cooling rates by up to 300% depending on the radiation field used. We also discovered that a model of radiation fields from stars and dust grain glow provided the best fit to observed data, particularly in the low-energy range. This finding suggests that a single radiation field model may not be sufficient to accurately represent the complex heating and cooling processes in the ISM. We introduce Fuel, a C++ framework that streamlines safe memory management, 
enabling developers to easily embed verified data structures into various applications. 
Fuel's framework leverages the type system to guarantee error-free operations and 
safely exploits memory through a type-driven approach, all while maintaining compatibility 
with the standard library and user-defined types. The innovative use of concept-based 
polymorphism in Fuel further enhances the framework's flexibility, allowing it to work 
seamlessly with both standard and user-defined types. In this paper, we introduce Fuel's 
key features and demonstrate its effectiveness in maintaining memory safety, 
encompassing protection against null pointer dereferences, use-after-free, and memory 
leaks, all of which are effectively addressed through static analysis. The performance of 
Fuel is also comparable to or better than existing verification tools. The framework's 
evaluation is further validated through a comprehensive benchmark suite that evaluates 
its scalability. The Fuel framework is available online at https://github.com/SeversonD/Fuel.

A major challenge in the field of Visual Question Answering lies in the domain generalization problem. This occurs because most current VQA approaches rely heavily on extensive training data, which can lead to overfitting when new domains are encountered. To address this issue, we introduce RAMEN, a novel framework that enables models to adapt effectively across various domains. RAMEN achieves this through a two-part approach: (1) a module that generates synthetic training data, and (2) a module that identifies areas of uncertainty using the domain-specific validation data. By producing synthetic data that closely resembles real data, RAMEN enables the model to learn more effectively from the training set. Meanwhile, the uncertainty estimation module allows the model to recognize instances where the synthetic data is insufficient, thereby preventing overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate that RAMEN outperforms existing state-of-the-art domain generalization methods on the CLEVR domain, as well as on the more extensive and complex GQA domain, with significant improvements in accuracy. Cox proportional hazards models with time-varying covariates are frequently used in mortality forecasting due to their flexibility in capturing changing mortality trends. A time-varying factor approach is proposed to accommodate shifting factor loadings while maintaining model parsimony. This method is particularly useful for long-term forecasts and allows for the identification of influential factors. Notably, our findings suggest that time-invariant factor loadings can effectively explain long-term forecasting requirements. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using US mortality data and examine the relationship between factor loadings and long-term mortality forecasts. The results show that the proposed model outperforms a traditional Cox model with time-varying hazard rates in terms of mean squared error. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the Cox model with time-varying hazard rates tends to overestimate mortality in the near future but underestimate it for longer-term projections. The findings offer insights into the drivers of long-term mortality trends and provide guidance for actuaries and demographers seeking a balance between model complexity and forecasting accuracy. Future research could explore alternative factor models with different estimation techniques to further refine mortality forecasts. Ultimately, our study contributes to the development of reliable long-term mortality forecasts that account for the complexities of mortality trends. The proposed method demonstrates superior results in intense exercise video rate estimation compared to current methods, as validated by a large dataset of 1,255 real-time video clips of individuals performing various activities like running, cycling, and skiing. Making Interference Structures Explicit (MICE) is a widely used method for handling missing value data. In its standard implementation, each step of the cycle is conducted as multiple imputation through linear regression, utilizing a sparse pattern of the incomplete data. This approach can be problematic when the relationship between the variables involves many variables rather than just a few relevant ones, which can result in poor imputations. We suggest an alternative approach to addressing this issue within the MICE framework by incorporating principal component regression, where each step of the cycle is implemented using a type of principal component regression that takes into account a large number of variables. Our findings based on simulations indicate that this approach outperforms the standard MICE strategy, particularly in large datasets. Additionally, we demonstrate its application in a real-world example. Our code has been made available in the R package pcrgaz. This research was initiated in response to a request from the Dutch Statistics Netherlands to investigate the effects of using sparse multiple imputation in the context of a survey on education. This initial research led to a broader investigation into addressing the "many variables" problem in MICE, ultimately resulting in the development of the pcrgaz package. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to discussions within the missing data community about the most effective approaches to addressing this problem. Ultimately, we aim for our findings to be incorporated into future updates of the R package MICE. Deep learning models have been linked to discriminatory outcomes in various fields. One major challenge is that the training process of these models can actually increase bias, even when initial representations are designed to be fair. Traditional methods that incorporate fairness into representations are often limited to specific scenarios or require users to make difficult trade-offs between accuracy and fairness. In an effort to address these limitations, we have developed a new method that can improve fairness without compromising accuracy across a wide range of applications. This method is based on a neural network that can automatically learn fair representations by suppressing bias and reducing complexity. Our approach, which we call DAMFRE, uses a stacking and dampening technique to achieve this, and we have tested its effectiveness on various datasets, including the MNIST, Adult, and COMPAS. Our results show that DAMFRE significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both fairness and accuracy. Specifically, it reduces bias by 50-80% and achieves accuracy gains of up to 5% compared to the state-of-the-art approach. Additionally, we have demonstrated that DAMFRE can be used to identify and mitigate bias in existing models, and we have shown that it can also be applied to deep learning models with multiple layers. Our results demonstrate that DAMFRE is a powerful tool for achieving both accuracy and fairness in deep learning models, and we believe that it has the potential to become a standard approach in this field. Our results show that this approach can be effectively integrated into language models, leading to improved performance in tasks such as mathematical problem-solving and text summarization. Furthermore, we found that this approach can also enhance the accuracy of language comprehension, particularly in cases where the input contains errors. Overall, our findings suggest that semantic grounding can play a crucial role in improving the reliability of language models, and our research provides a foundation for future investigations into the capabilities and limitations of language models. A groundbreaking approach for detecting atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) involves using CT scans to measure coronary artery calcium. Despite its potential, the lack of standardization in processing methods hinders its reliability. To address this issue, we developed a fully automated system for accurate and reliable calcium scoring, and made it freely available to the research community. Our system, which includes both training data and source code, is designed to promote reproducibility and serve as a benchmark for future studies. By using a generative adversarial network to process CT scans, we achieved high accuracy in our testing data, and also demonstrated the versatility of our model by showing its effectiveness on unseen data from different scanners. As an effort to promote transparency and research in this field, the model, training data, and evaluation software are being made publicly accessible. Spiking neural networks have gained popularity due to their ability to mimic biological processes and efficient operation. However, the traditional backpropagation algorithm used to train SNNs has limitations, particularly when applied to spiking-based networks. To overcome these constraints, researchers have employed surrogate functions and gradient-based learning rules to simulate spike responses. Although this approach has some benefits, it can lead to gradient instability and inaccurate representations of true network dynamics. To address these issues, this study introduces two techniques: gradient regularization and activation normalization, which are designed to enhance the reliability and accuracy of gradient-based learning in SNNs. Through experiments on various neural networks, the proposed methods have been shown to significantly improve the performance of SNNs trained via gradient ascent. Moreover, the researchers have made their code publicly available to facilitate further exploration and improvement of SNNs. This study serves as a step towards developing more efficient SNNs that can replace traditional ANNs in real-world applications. Complex Bayesian hierarchical models can be computationally demanding due to the high cost of the full posterior distribution calculation, making Approximate Bayesian Inference crucial for efficient computations.  R-INLA is a widely-used tool that employs a hierarchical approximation strategy, referred to as the Simplified Laplace (sLap) approach, for computing accurate enough approximations of the posterior distributions of the intrinsic latent variables.  This paper presents an extension of the sLap method that takes into account the posterior distribution of the hyperparameters, providing a more comprehensive solution.  The proposed approach is implemented in R-INLA and demonstrated through a series of numerical examples that showcase its effectiveness in scenarios where traditional sLap fails.  The results highlight the advantages of the new method in terms of its ability to provide accurate approximations even in scenarios with complex hyperparameter priors.  The proposed approach is particularly useful in cases where the full hyperparameter posterior distribution is of interest. This study addresses the challenge of obtaining a solution to a specific stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) with a singular nonlinearity, for which the conditions of the local well-posedness based on the stochastic flow method cannot be met due to the non-summability of the singular term. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel renormalized approach that allows us to remove the divergent terms from the nonlinearity and establish local and global well-posedness under significantly weaker summability conditions. This research draws inspiration from the recent work of Gubinov and Kupcov, as well as its adaptation by Masmoudi, who adapted the probabilistic method to tackle SPDEs with singularities in the leading term. Our key contributions include the development of a novel renormalization strategy, enabling the application of the probabilistic approach to SPDEs with singularities in the subleading term for the first time. This research also presents a novel method of proof for the renormalization of stochastic equations, based on the concept of the stochastic flow, and is applicable to both deterministic and stochastic settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the local and global well-posedness of the SPDE in question under the conditions of the regularity of the initial condition and the logarithmic summability of the singular term. Additionally, we show that the solution exhibits a pathwise Hölder regularity of the index 1/2 in the global case. This research has significant implications for the study of the KPZ equation, for which the conditions of the local and global well-posedness have been established under the conditions of the almost sure local integrability of the solution. Consequently, we obtain almost sure global well-posedness of the KPZ equation under the conditions of the logarithmic integrability of the solution. Go's growing popularity as a scalable concurrency language makes it crucial to develop efficient binary analysis tools for detecting bugs in Go programs. We introduce BinGo, a static analyzer specifically designed for Go binary formats, which identifies five common concurrency bugs: deadlock, lock time-out, lock starvation, resource leak, and use-after-free. By leveraging a unique inter-procedure control flow model, enhanced with a stack frame graph, and a fast string analysis, BinGo overcomes challenges posed by Go's high-level features. We evaluate BinGo on a diverse set of Go programs and show its ability to detect bugs accurately and efficiently. Our results indicate that BinGo can analyze large programs within minutes and outperforms existing tools in both bug detection and speed. In this study, we explore multi-armed bandit problems with sequential arm selections that adhere to monotonicity, which is a common real-world constraint found in various applications like personalized web pages and online advertising systems. We introduce a new algorithm, monotone UCB, that is capable of achieving a time complexity of O(T^(1+1/(2+2*beta+1/(2*beta+1)))). This proposed method is notable for its optimality, requiring a minimum of (beta+1)/(2*beta+1) additional time steps compared to the well-known UCB algorithm. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the problem's time complexity, demonstrating that monotone UCB is asymptotically optimal. Notably, this study presents the first instance where a lower bound is proven for a multi-armed bandit problem with specific constraints. Furthermore, we propose a new family of algorithms called UCB-Mod, which is capable of achieving a time complexity of O(Tbeta), and is particularly effective when beta is an integer value. This proposed method is particularly useful in the context of learning with restricted arm sequences and is demonstrated through extensive numerical simulations. This paper explores a key problem concerning the volume of the Minkowski sum of multiple zonoids. Notably, we will demonstrate two essential properties. Firstly, the convex hull of the Minkowski sum of various zonoids is equivalent to the Minkowski sum of their convex hulls. Secondly, under specific conditions, the Minkowski sum of zonoids can be replaced by the Minkowski sum of their exterior zones in order to compute their volumes. These findings will be utilized to develop an iterative method for calculating the volume of the Minkowski sum of any number of simple, convex polytopes. This approach will be validated through several numerical examples. Additionally, we will discuss the extension of this method to determine the volumes of the intersection and union of simple, convex polytopes. Furthermore, we will present a generalization of Alexandrov's theorem, applicable to the volume functional within the set of all symmetric, convex bodies in n-dimensional space. Lastly, we will provide an asymptotic formula for calculating the volume of the Minkowski sum of a specific type of convex body in n-dimensional space for large volumes. This formula will be validated through numerical examples. The primary contribution of this paper lies in its development of an iterative method for calculating the volume of the Minkowski sum of simple, convex polytopes and its practical applications. This method represents a significant breakthrough in the field of convex geometry. The Alexandrov's theorem generalization and volume sum replacement results are novel and have the potential to facilitate further research in this field. The proposed asymptotic formula is a valuable contribution to the existing literature on convex geometry. The numerical examples presented in this paper demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed methods. By utilizing a cost function that is differentiable with respect to camera positions, the approach is able to efficiently estimate these positions. The proposed approach is shown to be efficient and robust through numerical experiments. The results indicate that the method is robust to noise and capable of handling complex viewing graphs with numerous camera positions and orientations. The integration of diverse renewable energy sources into the power grid has
complicated the task of determining the necessary reserve capacity, a challenge
further complicated by the uncertainty associated with renewable energy
predictions. To address this challenge, a novel approach is proposed that uses
probabilistic forecasts to calculate the reserve needs in real-time, thus allowing
for immediate adjustments in response to changing conditions. To validate this
methodology, a simulation model was created, set in a hypothetical power grid based
on data from a real grid, resulting in a significant reduction in reserve requirements
of up to 30 percent, a finding that highlights the potential of operating real-time
reserve determinations. Additionally, this study examines the trade-offs between the
types of reserves used, the reserve capacity provided by different power plants, and
the reserve requirements for various grid locations, thus providing valuable insights
into the complex relationships influencing power grid operations."

flexible materials, which in turn significantly affect their behavior. To simplify
the simulation of these systems, researchers often use reduced-order models that
approximate the system's complex dynamics by focusing on its most critical aspects.

successfully applied to various systems, but its limitations in capturing certain
dynamic phenomena have become apparent. To address this, a new reduced-order
model, the Piecewise Affine Curvature model, has been developed. This new model
builds upon an existing approach, the Affine Curvature Container, by incorporating
a more general representation of curvature and allowing it to be piecewise affine.
The proposed model retains the benefits of its predecessor while providing a more
flexible framework for simulating complex systems, including those with distinct
dynamic behaviors. To validate its effectiveness, researchers have successfully
applied this new model to various systems, including a flexible rod interacting with
a wall, and found it to be in close agreement with more detailed simulations. The
success of this new model suggests its potential as a valuable tool for understanding
and simulating soft robot-environment interactions. Furthermore, it is anticipated
that this reduced-order model will be instrumental in creating more accurate and
realistic simulations of these systems, thus paving the way for new discoveries and
advances in the field. The code implementing this new reduced-order model is now
available for public use. Although this new model has been specifically developed
with soft robots in mind, it is versatile enough to be applied to a wide range of
other systems, including those involving rigid and fluidic components. The

This research introduces a non-parametric method to quantify the impact of
a treatment on a target population, considering the effects of unobserved
confounding factors specific to distinct sub-populations. Building on previous
double machine learning studies, our approach combines double machine learning
estimators with targeted mediation analysis to estimate the direct and indirect
effects of a treatment. Through simulations, we compare our method to a
parametric approach and assess its performance in real-world applications,
such as analyzing the relationship between hospital entry and post-infection
mortality in patients with pneumonia. Our findings suggest that double machine
learning can effectively account for the impact of confounding factors, but
may overestimate indirect effects if not applied correctly. Furthermore, our
research highlights the importance of considering potential biases in double
machine learning causal mediation analysis, such as the impact of model
specification, sample size, and the accuracy of double machine learning
estimators. To mitigate these biases, we recommend the use of non-parametric
methods that are less susceptible to model misspecification and data quality
issues. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the value of non-parametric
causal mediation analysis in accounting for the impact of unobserved
confounding factors, particularly in high-dimensional settings where model
specification is uncertain. This approach can be applied to a wide range of
fields, such as epidemiology, social sciences, and economics, where causal

facilitate the implementation of our method, we have developed an open-source

We also explore the broader implications of quantum computing on cryptography systems, highlighting the need for more secure encryption protocols. 
Our analysis concludes that, while quantum improvements are possible, they come with significant energy and technical challenges, rendering quantum computing a double-edged sword for cryptocurrency mining. 
In the end, we discuss the future prospects of quantum mining and its potential impact on the cryptocurrency landscape.

The dynamics of opinion formation within social networks are crucial to democracy, yet many current networks tend to polarize opinions due to their structure. To counteract this, we've developed an algorithm that optimizes exposure to opposing viewpoints, taking into account individual differences in how people react to conflicting information, specifically the potential for it to solidify or erode convictions. The proposed algorithm balances multiple factors, including the strength of opposing viewpoints, individual sensitivities, and network structure, to effectively mitigate polarization. When applied to random networks, our algorithm demonstrates its ability to reduce polarization and accommodate varying levels of sensitive individuals, all without requiring the identification of individual opinions. To validate our approach, we compare its effectiveness with a baseline strategy of randomly selecting network nodes and find that it produces superior results across various scenarios. The algorithm's potential for real-world application is also explored, with potential use cases including designing more effective social networks or developing personalized algorithms to counteract the influence of biased sources. Furthermore, we've developed a Python implementation that can efficiently process large social networks. When applied to a social network of 1000 individuals with 20 distinct clusters, our algorithm achieves significant polarization reduction while maintaining reasonable computational efficiency. Current video conferencing systems struggle with video quality due to limited upload bandwidth, necessitating the use of video compression. However, the existing quality metrics and codecs often fail to meet the requirements of conversational content, resulting in an unacceptably high rate of poor-quality video frames. Recent neural networks have shown potential in improving video quality, but they are not suitable for real-time conferencing due to their resource-intensive nature. This research proposes a novel neural network framework called Gemino that addresses these issues by combining the benefits of previous approaches. By integrating multiple modules, Gemino offers a scalable solution for high-quality video compression, enabling efficient processing on various devices while maintaining high video quality and minimizing bitrate. Our experiments demonstrate that Gemino significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of video quality and robustness to varying conditions. Furthermore, the integration of Gemino into a live video conferencing system results in a substantial reduction in poor-quality video frames by 2.5 times and a 30% reduction in upload bandwidth, all while maintaining the same level of quality. The neutrino flux from neutron star mergers can be significantly reduced due to flavor instabilities caused by the rapid evolution of the outflow's temperature and composition.  This phenomenon is crucial for modeling the electromagnetic and chemical evolution of the merger, particularly in terms of the nucleosynthesis processes involved. This study investigates the performance of these metrics, particularly in relation to the evolution of the outflow's temperature and composition.  Our findings indicate that the most accurate metrics are those that consider the temperature and entropy distributions within the range of the local equilibrium solution.  However, these metrics may not be sufficient for accurately predicting flavor instabilities in neutron star mergers, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive approach that incorporates a deeper understanding of the outflow's complex dynamics. This second paper in a two-part series introduces a novel modulation technique called orthogonal time frequency space modulation (OTFS), which effectively transmits information during high-mobility wireless communications. Building upon the first paper's foundational concepts, this article focuses on designing transceiver components for OTFS systems. OTFS's unique time-frequency structure is first analyzed to derive an appropriate signal propagation model suitable for diverse wireless environments. Subsequently, two detection methods - maximum likelihood detection and linear minimum mean square error detection - are developed and evaluated through simulation results, demonstrating their respective performance in different channel conditions. Ultimately, OTFS's design is enhanced by incorporating low-order modulations and power control strategies, resulting in a robust and efficient transmission method. Simulation results indicate that OTFS's performance is significantly better than existing techniques such as WSR and UF-OFDM under similar conditions. Moreover, this article presents simulation outcomes that demonstrate OTFS's ability to achieve high data transfer rates and low error rates across a variety of wireless channels. The final section of this two-part paper outlines future research opportunities and potential avenues for exploring OTFS's capabilities in new and innovative ways. This document outlines a preliminary specification for the Black Box, a novel
standard enabling independent assessment of behaviour in robots. As robots become
increasingly integrated into daily life, there is a growing need for accountability
and transparency in their actions. The Black Box, under development, will allow
independent evaluation of social robots' behaviour, complementing existing
initiatives. For social robots to gain widespread acceptance, we must ensure their
actions align with human values, with the Black Box serving an essential role in
making this possible. The draft Open Standard presented here is a key step towards
establishing a universally applicable specification for the Black Box, which we
hope will engage stakeholders and inform future development. The development of the
Black Box is an ASHES project, supported by the European Horizon 2020 program.

The adversarial robustness-accuracy tradeoff has gained significant attention in computer vision and robotics research. Despite its importance, the concept remains poorly understood in the context of robot learning. This paper aims to clarify this issue by revisiting the relationship between adversarial robustness and accuracy from a robotics perspective. We examine the current limitations of robotics research in this area and propose a structured approach to addressing the ARAT issue in robotics. We identify key challenges and opportunities for robotics to integrate robust learning principles into real-world applications. Furthermore, we discuss the importance of considering the entire robot learning pipeline, including learning algorithms, to address the ARAT problem. We highlight the need for more robust datasets and models, as well as the development of novel learning algorithms tailored to robotics. Finally, we discuss the potential benefits of robust learning in robotics and outline future research directions. We hope that this paper will inspire innovative research in robotics and provide a foundation for developing more robust learning algorithms. Recent advancements in pre-trained models have led to significant breakthroughs in various vision and language tasks. However, the current state of pre-training for Chinese video and language remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, this paper proposes a novel pre-training framework that leverages contrastive learning to bridge the knowledge gap between Chinese video and language. By integrating a multimodal encoder with a contrastive pre-training method, the proposed framework enables the learning of complex semantic relationships between Chinese video and language. To evaluate the proposed framework's performance, we introduce a new dataset, the Chinese Video and Language Pre-training (CVLP) dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on CVLP, surpassing existing models by 2.2% and 3.1% in video-language retrieval and video-title retrieval tasks, respectively. achieves a high mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) score of 46.8% on the
Carla dataset, surpassing the previous best score of 32.9%. Our analysis and
results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our open-source code

In object recognition, a significant challenge is open-set recognition, which involves identifying objects that fall outside a predefined set of known classes. This issue is often encountered in real-world applications where unknown categories can impact performance. Traditional methods for open-set recognition typically rely on a known class set and an unknown category label. However, a more realistic scenario is when the class labels are unavailable, forcing the system to reject unfamiliar inputs. This paper proposes a novel approach to open-set recognition, utilizing a similarity metric to evaluate input similarity. This metric is based on a learned similarity function that measures the distance between feature vectors, taking advantage of the augmentation-based similarity learning framework. By leveraging multiple viewpoints through image augmentation, the method can effectively capture object nuances and improve performance. Experimental results on standard datasets demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over existing approaches. Additionally, the method's generalizability is evaluated by applying it to unseen datasets without their class labels, showcasing its potential in real-world applications. We've investigated how time-delayed optical feedback affects the behavior of a microlaser with resonant frequencies. By applying this feedback near a specific frequency, we've observed a phenomenon where multiple tongues can merge into a single one when the excitable microlaser operates within a certain parameter range. Conversely, we've also shown that an existing tongue can split apart and re-emerge when the parameters are adjusted further, resulting in a periodic pattern that transitions into a state of complete laser stabilization. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that this transition can occur through an intermediate regime characterized by a 'locked phase' where the laser oscillations are synchronized but not perfectly stable. Notably, we've also identified a 'borderline' where the laser exhibits a unique combination of oscillation frequencies that are both in and out of phase with one another. Our findings provide new insights into how delayed optical feedback influences the behavior of microlasers and open the door to controlling their resonant frequencies through experimental means.
